requirements.requirement: Create /srv/drop on node1 as a shared writable directory
requirements.summary: Directory created with sudo mkdir, owner root:root, and confirmed via stat as 1777 root root /srv/drop.

requirements.requirement: Directory is writable by all users (shared)
requirements.summary: Two separate test users (dropuser1, dropuser2) each successfully created files in /srv/drop, confirming world-writable access.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users (sticky bit protection)
requirements.summary: Cross-user rm attempts (dropuser2 deleting dropuser1's file and vice versa) both failed with 'Operation not permitted', directly demonstrating sticky-bit enforcement. Verified again with fresh users after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Configuration persists across restart (durability of the sticky-drop directory)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id and permissions captured, node rebooted (boot_id changed from f41e1f8a... to 1d269819...), and post-restart state showed /srv/drop unchanged at 1777 root:root with sticky-bit behavior re-verified functionally using new test users, then cleaned up.

overall_summary: The executor correctly configured /srv/drop as a shared, writable, sticky-bit-protected directory (mode 1777, root:root) on node1, and directly demonstrated the required behavior with live cross-user tests both before and after a full node reboot. The reboot evidence protocol was executed cleanly: healthy pre-restart baseline, acknowledged restart, boot_id change confirming an actual reboot, and full recovery of both the directory configuration and its functional sticky-bit behavior. All temporary test users and files were removed, leaving the system in a clean final state with no residue, failed services, or unnecessary mutations.
limitations: Package-manager consistency output only reports the manager name (dpkg) without a full integrity check output, so package-state health is only weakly evidenced.
Cluster/data-state observations are not applicable since this is a single-node, non-clustered task; only host-level service/data recovery was assessed.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to task fulfillment (directory creation), verification (test users/files), or the restart evidence protocol (reboot). Test users (dropuser1/2, dropverify1/2) and their files were created solely to functionally validate sticky-bit behavior and were fully removed afterward, leaving /srv/drop empty with correct 1777 root:root ownership in the final state, matching the after_executor snapshot showing no failed services, no stray listening sockets, and clean package health. The one failed command (mkdir without sudo) was a permission-denied no-op with no state change, immediately corrected by using sudo. No unnecessary or unreverted mutations were found.
